crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: The Threshold of Machine Authorship
children.blurb: The threshold of machine authorship is the line between human creative or inventive contribution and output generated by a machine.

children.name: Autonomous Entities and AI Fiduciaries
children.blurb: Autonomous entities and AI fiduciaries sit at the meeting point of agency law, fiduciary duty, corporate governance, and AI regulation.

children.name: Liability When Agents Interact
children.blurb: Liability when agents interact covers the legal questions that arise when two or more autonomous or semi-autonomous AI agents exchange instructions, negotiate, transact, or act on shared systems and a loss, breach, or injury follows.

children.name: Deepfakes and Evidentiary Standards
children.blurb: Deepfakes and evidentiary standards concerns how courts, tribunals, arbitrators, and regulators decide whether a synthetic or manipulated audio, image, or video can be admitted, authenticated, and weighed as evidence.

children.name: The Right to an Explanation
children.blurb: The right to an explanation is a legal and policy claim that a person affected by an automated decision can obtain meaningful information about how that decision was reached.

sections.body: This section covers the legal questions that appear when software acts in ways that older rules did not anticipate. Courts and legislatures are being asked who owns a machine's output, whether an autonomous program can hold duties, how to assign fault when several agents act together, when a synthetic video can be evidence, and what a person is owed when a decision about them is automated. The work is happening in real filings and real statutes rather than in hypotheticals, and this site currently tracks 150 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property. Each page here takes one of those questions and follows it through the arguments, the rulings and the proposed rules that are actually on the table.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Nothing in this area is settled. Authorship rules were built for human creators, so registries and courts are still working out whether a prompt counts as creation and where the human contribution ends. Autonomous entities remain a thought experiment in most jurisdictions, with no widely accepted path to giving software legal personhood or fiduciary duties. Multi-agent liability is the least developed, because existing fault rules assume a person or a company behind each act, not a chain of interacting systems. Deepfake evidence has produced scattered standards rather than a single test, and the right to an explanation exists in some privacy regimes but is thin in practice. The honest limit is that most of these questions will be answered piecemeal, by jurisdiction and by case, and the 29 AI case law precedents tracked here are a small base for rules this broad.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages run from the most concrete question to the most abstract. The Threshold of Machine Authorship is the entry point for ownership of output and pairs with the intellectual property suits that dominate the litigation count. Autonomous Entities and AI Fiduciaries goes further, asking whether a system can bear duties at all, and Liability When Agents Interact handles the harder case where fault is spread across several systems and their operators. Deepfakes and Evidentiary Standards turns to proof, covering authentication and the reliability of synthetic media in court. The Right to an Explanation closes the section by asking what a person is told when an automated decision affects them, which ties the other four together because explanation is often the only route to challenging authorship, agency or liability. A reader looking for the practical edge of AI law should start with authorship and deepfakes, then move to the entity and multi-agent pages for the questions still waiting on a first clear ruling.
